\section{Introduction}
Flood forecasting in mountainous basins relies on conceptual
rainfall-runoff models whose parameters cannot be measured directly.
The Xinanjiang model, developed for humid and semi-humid regions of
China, remains a standard tool for such basins because its saturation
excess mechanism reproduces the observed nonlinearity of the runoff
response with few parameters.

Despite its widespread use, the model is routinely calibrated against
short streamflow records, and the resulting parameter sets are known to
be only weakly identifiable. Very different parameter combinations may
reproduce the calibration record equally well while diverging in
prediction.

This paper quantifies the predictive uncertainty of the model for the
upper Jinhua basin, a 230~km$^2$ catchment in Zhejiang province.
Section~2 reviews the model structure, Section~3 describes the
calibration strategy, and Section~4 presents the formulation used in
the uncertainty analysis.

\section{Model Overview}
The Xinanjiang model partitions the catchment into a tension water
storage and a free water storage. Evapotranspiration depletes the
tension water storage first, and runoff is generated only where the
tension water capacity is satisfied.

The spatial variability of the tension water capacity is represented by
a distribution curve with shape parameter $b$. For $b = 0$ the capacity
is uniform over the catchment, while larger values of $b$ concentrate
storage in a small fraction of the area. Typical calibrated values for
humid catchments lie between 0.1 and 0.4.

Free water is routed through three linear reservoirs representing
surface flow, interflow, and groundwater flow. The recession constants
of the three reservoirs control the shape of the simulated hydrograph
recession.

\section{Calibration}
Daily streamflow records from 2010 to 2020 at the basin outlet were
split into a calibration period (2010--2016) and a validation period
(2017--2020). Parameters were sampled with a Latin hypercube design of
20{,}000 points within ranges reported by previous studies of humid
catchments.

Each sampled parameter set was scored with the Nash--Sutcliffe
efficiency computed on daily flows. Parameter sets above the informal
threshold of 0.75 were retained as behavioural, yielding 1{,}340
behavioural sets out of the 20{,}000 samples.

The behavioural sets reproduce the calibration record well, but their
predictions diverge markedly during the largest validation events,
which motivates the variance decomposition presented in the next
section.

\section{Model Formulation}
For the uncertainty analysis we write the model in state-space form.
Let $S_t$ denote the tension water storage at time step $t$, and let
$P_t$ and $E_t$ denote precipitation and potential evapotranspiration.
The storage balance is
\begin{equation}
S_{t+1} = S_t + P_t - R_t - E_t \, f(S_t),
\end{equation}
where $R_t$ is the generated runoff and $f(S_t)$ is the depletion
function implied by the distribution curve.

The simulated discharge at the outlet is $Q_t = \alpha Q_{t-1} +
\beta R_t + \gamma B_t where $\alpha$ is the combined recession
coefficient, $\beta$ maps generated runoff to discharge, and $B_t$ is
the baseflow contribution from the groundwater reservoir.

The variance of the predictive distribution is decomposed with a
first-order sensitivity index computed from the behavioural ensemble.
